newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian stocks drop seen producing some jewels.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian stocks drop seen producing some jewels.

text.p: An already shaky Kuala Lumpur share market shed more than 3 percent on Monday on Wall Street's drop, but analysts said there were still good values to be found.

Fund managers say they are not selling because of the decline and instead are urging clients to pick up attractively valued stocks in industries like consumer products, construction and financial services.
Following the 2.3 percent-tumble in the Dow on Friday, Malaysian blue chips ended at midday on Monday down 33.33 points, or 2.93 percent, at 1,105.03.
The decline continued after the break and by 0644 GMT, the index had fallen 38.70 points, or 3.40 percent, to 1099.70.
"The Dow definitely made the sentiment worse," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager at TA Asset Management. "I think the problem is that the buyers have just simply disappeared."

Bulls in the Kuala Lumpur bourse had already been scarce since the central bank's restrictions on property and stock lending at the end of March raised questions about profits in both sectors. From March 28 through Friday, Malaysian stocks dropped 6.5 percent.

Malaysia's move to curb speculation in the property market followed similar actions in neighbouring Thailand and Singapore. The Philippines' stock market has also been convulsed by fear of a property glut.
"A few panic sellers can really spook the market," said Simon Maughan, head of research at W.I. Carr. "The biggest problem is in convincing people that they should buy now."

He said stocks he still recommends are in the "emerging blue chip" group, such as car distributor Edaran Otomobil Nasional Bhd (EON). Valuing EON just on its motor business, the stock is selling at a 40 percent discount to its peers.
Other stocks he recommends are insurer Malaysian Assurance Alliance Bhd, construction firm Road Builder (M) Holdings Bhd, and Malaysia Mining Corp Bhd.
"The Kuala Lumpur market had a good year last year (so) that people have forgotten things can get bad again," said Robert Coombe, executive director of Commerce Asset Fund Managers.
"Our advice to investors is to hold in there. We're not anticipating a crash, but it's going to be a saw-tooth pattern emerging in the next two to three months," he said.
Coombe said some sectors his firm is investing in are so-called defensive industries -- those whose earnings are resilient through economic cycles -- like consumer goods makers and utilities.
But investors should be picky, he said. Compared with other regional markets, "Malaysia is not cheap", Coombe said.
Analysts say the Malaysian stock market is currently trading at around 18 to 20 times compared with historical levels of 20 to 21 times.
Ang said there are "lots of bargains" for investors who do not have to sell to cover leveraged positions.
"Some blue chips like Telekom have dropped," he said, adding that good second-liners include hotel and property firm Pernas International Holdings Bhd.
Other stocks he would buy are financial services firm Affin Holdings Bhd and construction concern Sungei Way Holdings Bhd.
